title: MSG Turned Off Its Controversial Cameras for Taylor Swift's Rehearsal Dinner
excerpt: Madison Square Garden's sprawling surveillance system can track guests down to the second. Its owners made a rare exception for the pop star's pre-wedding gathering, even as a leaked database reveals how the venue profiles and monitors celebrities.
body:
• Madison Square Garden briefly disabled its facial recognition and surveillance cameras for Taylor Swift's rehearsal dinner on July 2, according to WIRED — a privilege never extended to ordinary patrons or critics of owner James Dolan.
  • A leaked MSG database of nearly 40,000 names assigned "risk scores" to roughly 400 celebrities and labeled 93 entries as "LGBTQIA," prompting a defamation lawsuit against WIRED.
  • Hackers dumped 45 gigabytes of MSG data online, exposing how Dolan's surveillance empire extends from the Garden to the Sphere in Las Vegas and Radio City Music Hall.

The Cameras Go Dark — But Only for Swift

Madison Square Garden's sprawling surveillance system can monitor guests down to the second. It has tracked a trans woman's every movement through an 18-page, camera-by-camera report. It has banned lawyers, critics, and a mother attending a Rockettes show with her nine-year-old daughter. But when Taylor Swift held her rehearsal dinner at the venue's Infosys Theater on July 2, the arena's controversial cameras briefly went dark, according to WIRED.

MSG invested at least $6 million in metal detectors with built-in facial scanning cameras that capture every face entering its venues. The system enforces a ban list driven not by physical safety concerns but by social media criticism of Dolan, according to multiple WIRED investigations. Yet for Swift's intimate pre-wedding gathering of about 100 guests, the surveillance apparatus was temporarily disabled.

A Leaked Database Exposes MSG's Inner Workings

The camera exception is one detail in a broader scandal. In June, the hacker collective ShinyHunters breached MSG's systems and dumped 45 gigabytes of files online after Dolan refused to pay a ransom. The leaked data included a "talent database" of 39,539 entries — celebrities, politicians, media figures, and sports personalities.

Roughly 400 celebrities were assigned risk scores. Diehard Knicks fans Edie Falco and Ben Stiller were labeled "low risk." Rappers Freddie Gibbs, Lil Jon, and DaBaby were designated "high risk." Comedian Adam Pally was marked "not to be hosted" due to critical comments about the team's management.

"It's a really, really paranoid, terrible system."

— Source with knowledge of MSG's internal database, speaking to WIRED

The database also tracked celebrities' sexual orientation, with 93 entries labeled "LGBTQIA," including Ricky Martin and Phoebe Bridgers. Five identified attendees at Swift's July 3 wedding — Ice Spice, Selena Gomez, Benson Boone, Michael Strahan, and Mariska Hargitay — were marked "low risk."

MSG Sues WIRED; Legal Experts Are Skeptical

MSG filed a 40-page defamation lawsuit against WIRED on July 16, accusing the outlet of using stolen data "to manufacture a false narrative portraying MSG as targeting the LGBTQIA community for discriminatory purposes."

WIRED responded within hours: "We stand by this reporting, and plan to vigorously defend it against this baseless and ridiculous lawsuit." The outlet removed the paywall from two MSG stories, inviting the public to read "the MSG stories they don't want you to read."

"They just seem overly interested in queer and trans people in their venue."

— Evan Greer, director of Fight for the Future

Legal analysts say MSG faces steep hurdles. New York defamation law requires the court to assess the "whole story," and the statements in WIRED's reporting appear factually accurate. "The complaint seems like a waste of the court's time," wrote attorney Jack Greiner in the Cincinnati Enquirer.

A Personal Irony

In 2018, Swift deployed hidden facial recognition cameras at her Rose Bowl concert to scan fans for known stalkers, with images sent to a "command post" in Nashville. Eight years later, the venue she chose for her wedding runs one of the most aggressive civilian surveillance systems in the country — and made a rare exception to turn it off for her.

The leaked database has reignited calls for regulating facial recognition at private venues. A class-action lawsuit filed in June calls the breach a byproduct of Dolan's surveillance state. "A company that cannot secure a customer list has no business scanning our faces," said Darío Maestro, legal director of the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project. MSG's cameras are back on. Whether the venue can keep its own secrets is another matter.
nri_angle: The revelations raise questions about surveillance practices at major American venues frequented by Indian-American celebrities and fans.
author: Diaspora Desk
